name: 05_quarterly_performance_report_generation
raw_text:
Quarterly Performance Report Generation – Client
 Reporting Procedure
Sample enterprise SOP for workflow-extraction testing
1. Purpose and Scope
This procedure describes the preparation of quarterly portfolio performance reports for client distribution. It
covers the retrieval and validation of performance data, benchmark comparison, controlled disclosure
language, narrative commentary, report assembly and portfolio manager approval.
2. Reporting Period and Data Sources
At the close of each reporting quarter, the reporting team establishes the applicable reporting period and
identifies the approved data sources. Portfolio returns are obtained from the custodian or designated
performance system. Benchmark information is retrieved for the same period and checked against the
benchmark applicable to the portfolio.
3. Data Availability Check
The reporting analyst checks that the required portfolio and benchmark information is available. Missing or
inconsistent records are investigated using the established data-quality process. The report is not finalized
using an unverified value merely because a deadline is approaching.
4. Performance Calculation
Portfolio performance is calculated using the firm's established reporting methodology. The resulting return is
compared with the applicable benchmark return for the same period. Where additional standard metrics are
required by the reporting template, they are calculated using the approved methodology and stored with the
reporting data.
5. Data Review
The calculated figures are reviewed for unexpected changes, missing values or inconsistencies with the
source data. Any issue identified during this review is resolved before the figures are incorporated into the
final client report. The purpose of this review is to ensure that the numerical information presented to the
client is traceable to the approved source.


6. Controlled Disclosure Language
Quarterly reports contain standard risk disclosures and other approved boilerplate language. The reporting
team retrieves the current controlled version of the relevant template or disclosure library. The approved
wording is inserted into the appropriate sections without discretionary rewriting, because changes to
controlled disclosure language may require a separate review and approval process.
7. Portfolio Activity Review
The reporting analyst or portfolio manager reviews material portfolio activity during the quarter. Relevant
purchases, sales, allocation changes and other events are considered together with significant market
developments that affected portfolio results. The purpose is to identify the factors that are genuinely useful
for explaining the quarter to the client.
8. Narrative Performance Commentary
A written narrative is prepared to explain the principal drivers of performance in plain language. The
commentary may need to connect several sources of information, distinguish material drivers from incidental
events and present the explanation in a manner appropriate for the client. The reviewer checks that the
narrative is consistent with the reported figures and portfolio activity.
9. Report Assembly
The report combines the calculated performance figures, benchmark comparison, approved disclosure
language and narrative commentary. The reporting process places each component into the appropriate
section of the standard client-facing template. Formatting checks are performed before the document is
converted to its final PDF form.
10. Quality Review
The completed report is reviewed for numerical consistency, correct benchmark information, completeness
of disclosures and consistency between the narrative and the underlying portfolio activity. Errors identified
during the review are corrected before the report proceeds to final approval.
11. Portfolio Manager Sign-Off
The final report is submitted to the portfolio manager for review and sign-off. The manager considers the
overall presentation, performance commentary and material client-facing statements. If changes are
requested, the report is returned to the reporting team for revision and another review cycle.
12. Distribution and Record
After approval, the report is released through the established client distribution process. The approved
version is retained with the relevant reporting records. The reporting team maintains the source information
and final report so that the client-facing figures and commentary can be traced to the reporting period and
underlying evidence.

scores.reasoning: This quarter-end step follows a recurring pattern of defining the reporting period, retrieving returns and benchmark data, and checking the benchmark applicable to the portfolio. Judgment is limited to resolving source or applicability exceptions, while incorrect period or benchmark selection could materially affect an audited, client-facing performance report. The work is largely deterministic and better suited to controlled rules and data integrations than incremental AI reasoning.

The analyst repeatedly verifies required portfolio and benchmark records using an established data-quality process. The check is primarily procedural, with limited judgment because missing or inconsistent data follows defined investigation steps. Compliance sensitivity is modest: the control prevents unverified values entering a quarterly performance report, but it does not determine performance, breach status, or disclosures. AI offers limited incremental value beyond deterministic availability and consistency checks, although it could assist with routing exceptions.

The step repeatedly applies an established reporting methodology, compares portfolio and benchmark returns for the same period, and calculates approved standard metrics. These operations are largely deterministic, requiring little interpretive judgment, though errors could materially affect a quarterly client-facing performance report and therefore warrant control review. AI adds limited value beyond a validated calculation engine.

Data Review recurs in quarterly performance reporting, but assessing unexpected changes and inconsistencies in case-specific calculated figures and approved source data varies materially. Resolving missing or conflicting values requires contextual judgment and evidence tracing, making this a material client-reporting control. AI could assist with anomaly detection, missing-value identification, and source reconciliation, but exceptions require explainable investigation and human review before incorporation into the final report.

This step repeatedly retrieves a controlled template or disclosure library and inserts pre-approved wording into designated report sections. It prohibits discretionary rewriting, so judgment is minimal; compliance handling matters, but the step does not interpret disclosures or decide applicability. Deterministic version control and text insertion would generally outperform AI reasoning.

The review occurs quarterly but the relevant purchases, sales, allocation changes, and market developments differ by portfolio and period. It requires weighing evidence and determining which events genuinely explain client results, creating material interpretive and client-reporting risk. AI could assist with activity retrieval and evidence synthesis, but contextual accuracy, attribution, and human review remain necessary.

Although this commentary is prepared in every quarterly performance report, its interpretive work varies by portfolio: it connects multiple information sources, distinguishes material drivers from incidental events, explains results for the client, and checks consistency with reported figures and portfolio activity. This requires specialist judgment and carries significant client-reporting and fiduciary risk, while AI could assist with evidence synthesis and drafting under mandatory reviewer oversight.

Report Assembly repeatedly places calculated figures, benchmark comparisons, approved disclosures, and prepared commentary into standard sections, performs formatting checks, and converts the document to PDF. The work is highly procedural with limited interpretation, although client-facing formatting errors warrant basic controls. Deterministic document-generation tools likely provide more reliable automation than AI, leaving limited incremental value for AI reasoning.

Quality Review recurs for each quarterly performance report, but it requires case-specific comparison of numerical results, benchmark information, disclosures, narrative, and portfolio activity. Resolving inconsistencies and correcting errors before Portfolio Manager Sign-Off requires substantial expert judgment and carries significant client, mandate, audit, and disclosure risk. AI could assist with cross-checking and identifying discrepancies, but variable evidence and compliance-sensitive corrections require controlled human review.

Although sign-off occurs for each quarterly report, the portfolio manager must evaluate case-specific performance commentary, overall presentation, and material client-facing statements, applying contextual professional judgment. Errors could affect clients, fiduciary communications, and auditability, while AI may support review but cannot reliably replace accountable manager approval.

This final step recurs through an established client distribution process with standardized retention of the approved report, source information, reporting period, and underlying evidence. Execution is largely procedural after sign-off, requiring little interpretive judgment, but distribution controls and traceable records are audit- and client-sensitive. Deterministic workflow automation can reliably handle release, filing, metadata, and retention, leaving limited incremental value for AI reasoning.
